name: Abdominal Pain
source_guidance: Adapted from NHS 111 guidance on stomach ache and abdominal pain, and WHO guidance on surgical and obstetric emergencies.

questions.text: Has the person collapsed or fainted, or are they pale, sweaty, and cold?
Is the pain sudden and severe, or is the belly hard and very painful to touch?
Is there vomiting of blood, or black or bloody stool?
Could the person be pregnant, with pain on one side, vaginal bleeding, or pain in the shoulder tip?
Is the person unable to pass stool or wind, with a swollen belly and vomiting?
Is there fever with the pain, or did the pain start near the belly button and move to the lower right side?
Is there pain or burning when passing urine, with back pain or fever?
Has the pain come and gone for more than a week, with no other worrying signs?

emergency: Call 112 now, or get to the nearest hospital emergency department immediately.
Do not eat or drink anything in case surgery is needed.
Lie still in the most comfortable position.
Do not drive yourself. Ask someone to take you, or wait for the ambulance.
urgent: Go to a hospital or clinic today and be seen within the next few hours.
Avoid eating until seen. Small sips of water are fine.
Do not take strong painkillers that may hide the signs before a clinician checks you.
Call 112 if the pain becomes severe or the person faints.
routine: Book a clinic appointment within the next few days.
Keep a note of when the pain happens and what makes it better or worse.
Call back at once if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear.
self_care: The answers point to a mild cause such as indigestion or wind.
Rest, drink water, and eat small, light meals.
Avoid alcohol, fizzy drinks, and spicy or fatty food for a day or two.
Paracetamol can be taken as directed on the pack.
Call back at once if symptoms get worse or new symptoms appear.
